Fellow Patriot - Today is it.

Like Lindsey, I grew up in the back of a bar and liquor store, in one room. My parents worked every single day to make ends meet. There was no time for sickness and few vacations, because if the doors weren't open, no money was coming in.

clean_body: Election Day is today. Help me reach every voter — and fuel the fight still ahead — before midnight. | Fellow Patriot - Today is it. The Primary Special Election for the United States Senate seat here in South Carolina, I'm not a politician. I never expected to be running for office, and I never wanted to. I'm doing this because I'm answering President Trump's call to serve, and because I believe South Carolina deserves a fighter in the Senate. Like Lindsey, I grew up in the back of a bar and liquor store, in one room. My parents worked every single day to make ends meet. There was no time for sickness and few vacations, because if the doors weren't open, no money was coming in. That's the kind of work ethic I've carried my whole life, from running a state agency with 130 employees and a $90 million budget to turning it into a national model for helping people find work and live independently. I'm a mother, a grandmother, and a wife. I support the Right to Life. I believe in showing ID to vote. I oppose DEI. I stand for the national anthem, I believe our veterans are heroes, and I will always Back the Blue. President Trump wants a fighter in the Senate - that's why he's in my corner in this race, and why I'm asking you to be in it with me. Here's what I need from you right now, in the final hours before the polls close: If you live in South Carolina, make sure you vote today, and don't stop there. Call your friends, your family, your neighbors, your coworkers. Make sure they have a plan to get to the polls before midnight. Every vote we don't turn out tonight is a vote we can't get back. Every dollar raised today will help us build the momentum we need not only to win today but also to win in November. And I need to be honest with you: winning tonight is only the first step. After this Primary Special Election, we still have a long road ahead to the General Election, and this fight doesn't end when the polls close. I will need you again. But it starts with tonight. Help me finish strong. Thank you, Darline Graham P.S. I am the first woman United States senator in South Carolina history. Folks,
Just one week into the general election, we’ve been enjoying a daily barrage of good news, while John McGuire keeps stepping in it.
Since we clinched the nomination, I’ve been barnstorming the district, arm and arm with former candidate Dr. K, who I consider a dear friend. McGuire, on the other hand, is busy being torched by his primary opponent, Melanie Lucero, for being a “puppet” and “disappointment.”
https://secure.actblue.com/donate/perriello-em?amount=50 [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/perriello-em?amount=50]
Speaking of things my opponent is setting on fire: money.
McGuire blew $1.6 million to boost his primary race, and left himself cash-strapped. Now he’s begging the dark money corporate groups for more cash. And working families throughout the district have caught on to who McGuire really works for.
My campaign couldn’t be more different. Thanks to YOUR incredible, fired-up support, we’ve got the momentum. We’ve got a grassroots army that’s already knocking doors and spreading the good news – that we are going to reclaim Congress for the people!
Since you made me your nominee, I’ve been to every corner of the district. Mecklenburg and Lunenburg to Goochland and Louisa, Fluvanna and Buckingham to Danville to Lynchburg, and back to Charlottesville and Albemarle – and that’s just this week ! We’re not leaving a single stone unturned or a single voter un-talked to. We’re building a coalition of Democrats, Independents, and fed-up Republicans ready to restore our communities and our Constitution from the lunacy and corruption coming out of Washington.
And every single town I stop in, every single door I knock, stoop I sit on, diner I eat in, I hear the same thing: we’re ready to win, together.
https://secure.actblue.com/donate/perriello-em?amount=50 [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/perriello-em?amount=50]
We have been out in the community, helping to distribute book bags to kids headed back to school. Seeing our communities rally, even as McGuire has made everything more expensive for parents, keeps me going.
All of this is to say: we’ve got the momentum, and McGuire’s got a mess on his hands.
If you want to keep this going, consider making a grassroots contribution (or another, if you’ve already generously donated!) to build up my campaign for the general. We know MAGA is ready to pour millions of dollars into this race to protect their puppet and Trump’s rubber stamp, so we need to be prepared to counter their attacks with strong pushes of our own. [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/perriello-em?amount=50]
Thank you so much for being on this team and for every single thing you’ve done so far to help get us here. Together we will out-work, out-organize, and out-vote, and together we will win!
—Tom

Mecklenburg and Lunenburg to Goochland and Louisa, Fluvanna and Buckingham to Danville to Lynchburg, and back to Charlottesville and Albemarle – and that’s just this week ! We’re not leaving a single stone unturned or a single voter un-talked to. We’re building a coalition of Democrats, Independents, and fed-up Republicans ready to restore our communities and our Constitution from the lunacy and corruption coming out of Washington. And every single town I stop in, every single door I knock, stoop I sit on, diner I eat in, I hear the same thing: we’re ready to win, together. [] We have been out in the community, helping to distribute book bags to kids headed back to school. Seeing our communities rally, even as McGuire has made everything more expensive for parents, keeps me going. All of this is to say: we’ve got the momentum, and McGuire’s got a mess on his hands. If you want to keep this going, consider making a grassroots contribution (or another, if you’ve already generously donated!) to build up my campaign for the general. We know MAGA is ready to pour millions of dollars into this race to protect their puppet and Trump’s rubber stamp, so we need to be prepared to counter their attacks with strong pushes of our own. [] Thank you so much for being on this team and for every single thing you’ve done so far to help get us here. name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
subject: My generation is starting to be decisive at the polls.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for Congress
body:
#
When pundits do the “Monday Quarterbacking” and look at what demographics voted where in this insurgent wave, the generational tidal wave is often ignored.
Millennials are not punk kids anymore. We’re grown adults with mortgages and kids. My generation is starting to be decisive at the polls.
And there is real anger at having been ignored, sidelined, having our economic futures mortgaged by the generations that came before us — on everything from the economy to climate.
We’re taking the reins. And we know that we don't have to live like this anymore.

Friend, I need to be clear about what’s at stake in this election: **Medicaid. SNAP. Universal Childcare.**
**My Republican opponent has proposed cuts to all three.**
He’s taking his cues from Donald Trump, who has already made thousands of New Mexicans hungrier, sicker, and poorer. **_My opponent isn’t going to stop Donald Trump from cutting the very programs we need._**
**[_That’s why I need your help, friend. A new poll shows my Republican opponent 6 points ahead, and we cannot afford to take this election for granted. I’m running to protect Medicaid, SNAP, and Universal Childcare — programs that help New Mexico families afford healthcare, put food on the table, and give their kids a strong start. But I can’t win this race without you. Will you chip in $5 today to help me close the gap and protect these essential programs?_](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/15614?refcode=jtk1198-fr-nd&amount=5&t=2&akid=11667%2E400544%2E4jW7Gn)**

Friend, I’ve relied on Medicaid, SNAP, and WIC. I know what it’s like to work hard, stretch every dollar, and depend on these programs to make sure your family has what they need.
_My Republican opponent clearly doesn't._
Nearly half of New Mexicans rely on Medicaid. We have the highest SNAP participation rate of any state in the country. And since Universal Childcare was rolled out, more than 40,000 families have enrolled.
These programs make sure New Mexican families can get the healthcare they need, put healthy food on the table, and get the support they need to care for their children and go to work.
**These programs aren’t just worth protecting. They’re worth fighting for. Our families deserve the chance not just to get by, but to thrive.**
That’s why, alongside protecting Medicaid, SNAP, and Universal Childcare, I’ll fight to give New Mexicans a raise, make it easier for farmers and ranchers to sell their goods here at home, expand Universal Childcare, and strengthen our healthcare system by recruiting more nurses and doctors and making it more accessible to all New Mexicans, and so much more.
**I will never stop fighting to give New Mexicans the opportunity to get ahead and thrive.[_But if we’re going to meet this moment, we need the resources to win. So please, will you chip in $5 or whatever you can spare today to help me win this race, stop these cuts, and protect the programs New Mexico families rely on?_](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/15614?refcode=jtk1198-fr-nd&t=7&akid=11667%2E400544%2E4jW7Gn)**

These programs make sure New Mexican families can get the healthcare they need, put healthy food on the table, and get the support they need to care for their children and go to work. These programs aren’t just worth protecting. They’re worth fighting for. Our families deserve the chance not just to get by, but to thrive. That’s why, alongside protecting Medicaid, SNAP, and Universal Childcare, I’ll fight to give New Mexicans a raise, make it easier for farmers and ranchers to sell their goods here at home, expand Universal Childcare, and strengthen our healthcare system by recruiting more nurses and doctors and making it more accessible to all New Mexicans, and so much more. I will never stop fighting to give New Mexicans the opportunity to get ahead and thrive. | | Be fierce, Deb | | | | | |

The federal government spent $1.5 billion of your tax dollars to buy two ICE detention center facilities that it was already using, including Otay Mesa Detention Center right here in San Diego County.
https://timesofsandiego.com/immigration/2026/07/20/federal-government-purchase-otay-mesa-detention/ [https://timesofsandiego.com/immigration/2026/07/20/federal-government-purchase-otay-mesa-detention/]
The other facility is California City Detention Center, the largest ICE detention center in our state. Both were owned by CoreCivic, a private company, and as part of that deal, DHS purchased Otay Mesa for $739 million — even though it was recently valued at just $168 million. (And yes, Donald Trump owns stock in CoreCivic, but his blatant corruption is a whole other conversation.)
For now, CoreCivic is still running the facilities day to day, and we have a lot of unanswered questions about what this deal actually means. I’m deeply concerned it’s an attempt to ramp up local immigration detention, prevent Congressional oversight, and shield the government’s actions from public scrutiny and accountability.
But let me be super clear: changing the deed of who owns this detention center doesn’t change the obligation to treat every single person humanely, and respect their legal, civil, and human rights.
I’ve inspected Otay Mesa numerous times, both announced and unannounced.
At a recent visit, I raised concerns about medical, legal, and language access issues directly with ICE and CoreCivic representatives, pushing for answers on behalf of everyone in our community who has reached out and shared what they’ve seen and heard. I’m grateful to all the folks who’ve been calling and emailing my office — thank you!
I’m going to continue showing up and asking hard questions. Not just because conducting oversight is my job, but because our community deserves transparency, accountability, and dignity. ICE promised answers to my questions and concerns, and I’m going to hold them to it.
Our community deserves to know what is being done in our name. Because I don’t believe what this administration is doing is making us safer. In fact, it’s making us less safe.
Most of the people held at Otay Mesa are there because of civil violations, NOT violent crimes — but they were often violently detained by ICE agents in riot gear while at work, or arrested when they showed up at their immigration court hearings.
I’m not going to let a change in ownership at these horrific detention centers become an excuse to shut Congress out.
So while I keep pushing back, I ask that you keep it up, too. Keep showing up for your neighbors and speaking out against injustices — that’s how we make a difference right now.
– Sara

body:

A few months ago, my husband and I lost a pregnancy.
The physical toll was something not even my doctor prepared me for.
After 11 weeks of hope about bringing a new member into our family, we learned the pregnancy was no longer viable. After several weeks of bleeding and mourning, my doctor made clear that future pregnancy could be much more difficult if I didn't take medication to expel the retained miscarriage.
Like most women, I was told the medication would feel like a regular period. Maybe a little stronger cramping.
But when I took the medication, the pain was more intense than the pain I experienced delivering my son four years ago. I wasn't even advised to take it when my son was out of the house.
And I am not alone.
Women are routinely told that Ibuprofen is sufficient pain management during miscarriage. In practice, that's the functional equivalent of handing someone a stick to chew on.
Science and medicine have advanced in so many ways, but when it comes to reproductive health, the standard of care for women's pain in this country is still medieval.
I know there are broad differences in beliefs about reproductive health. But we do not need to agree on every policy question to agree that women should not have to endure excruciating pain while managing a miscarriage and protecting their ability to go on and bring a child into this world.
One in four women will likely experience a miscarriage. We can do better than telling them to take Ibuprofen and endure it.
That's why I introduced and passed a simple amendment directing the NIH to study strategies to improve pain management during miscarriage.

clean_body: ? [?] A few months ago, my husband and I lost a pregnancy. The physical toll was something not even my doctor prepared me for. After 11 weeks of hope about bringing a new member into our family, we learned the pregnancy was no longer viable. After several weeks of bleeding and mourning, my doctor made clear that future pregnancy could be much more difficult if I didn't take medication to expel the retained miscarriage. Like most women, I was told the medication would feel like a regular period. Maybe a little stronger cramping. But when I took the medication, the pain was more intense than the pain I experienced delivering my son four years ago. I wasn't even advised to take it when my son was out of the house. And I am not alone. Women are routinely told that Ibuprofen is sufficient pain management during miscarriage. In practice, that's the functional equivalent of handing someone a stick to chew on. Science and medicine have advanced in so many ways, but when it comes to reproductive health, the standard of care for women's pain in this country is still medieval. I know there are broad differences in beliefs about reproductive health. But we do not need to agree on every policy question to agree that women should not have to endure excruciating pain while managing a miscarriage and protecting their ability to go on and bring a child into this world. One in four women will likely experience a miscarriage. We can do better than telling them to take Ibuprofen and endure it. That's why I introduced and passed a simple amendment directing the NIH to study strategies to improve pain management during miscarriage. If you agree that women deserve better pain care than the status quo provides and that the Senate should pass this amendment, add your name today. [] ADD YOUR NAME [] We don't need to agree on everything to agree on this: Women who lose a pregnancy deserve compassion and dignity. ### The accelerating global climate catastrophe should be driving decisions at the local, national, and international level--yet neither elected leaders, nor journalists, nor even voters seem to care

Apologists for the status quo, including the president, have long argued that climate change is a "hoax." Events unfolding around the world should convincingly disprove them, but even as related calamities [continue](https://substack.com/redirect/01840d65-6abd-4813-8772-86685326846a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to destroy lives and [communities](https://substack.com/redirect/3320c73d-f2da-4c83-b785-1c0de5c49998?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), America's corporate political parties continue to drag humanity towards a meteorological abyss with limitless risks to human life & health.
### **A whole way worse than the sum of its parts**
At the same time that Asia is confronting [catastrophic flooding](https://substack.com/redirect/f33a592f-1c41-4bda-a5f7-18e8837aee88?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) driven by typhoons strengthened by global climate patterns, others--particularly the Pacific Northwest and western [Europe](https://substack.com/redirect/41bbf726-0bcf-4ba1-9200-712e3bca3d90?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--are battling [unprecedented wildfires](https://substack.com/redirect/767d7fe0-cc03-4956-b8b2-26af565e4749?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).

Either of these patterns would be bad enough. China has evacuated over a million people fleeing floods inundating major cities including Shanghai, while wildfires burning near Madrid and Paris have prompted alarm and anxiety across Europe.
The juxtaposition, however, suggests a whole far worse than the sum of its parts.
International agencies and non-profit organizations have spared no alarm. The United Nations Environment Programme, for instance, has noted that "The world may soon cross some potentially disastrous tipping points," and powerfully depicted the scale of climate chaos through [data visualizations](https://substack.com/redirect/af1b9c18-073a-4f0c-9719-7a28f7d2aedc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Yet, while these globally interlinked unfolding disasters have attracted worldwide attention and concern, the pattern that connects them continues to be effectively ignored by elected leaders and journalists across the United States.

### **A war making everything worse**
The war in Iran is offensive for many reasons. The [sheer imbecility](https://substack.com/redirect/55335f39-0b1a-46f3-ac67-219b62f966e5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that enabled it will be remembered by whatever vestiges of human civilization survive the next generation.
Its damage to the global economy continues to mount by the day.
But the relationship between war and the acceleration of climate chaos is, in fact, the dumbest thing about the whole sordid endeavor. Ultimately, the Pentagon is the Earth's [leading institutional consumer ](https://substack.com/redirect/d34f7135-9827-43ca-bf90-3383b22e3105?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)of fossil fuels, while its actions--particularly in the Middle East over the past six months--have made fossil fuels more scarce, and less secure to extract or ship.
Beyond this long applicable global analysis of the Pentagon's carbon footprint, Trump's war on Iran has also sparked an acute [global fertilizer shortage](https://substack.com/redirect/839dfdcd-3bb1-4db2-adef-a37d8c31a58c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) over the past six months, which has already done incalculable damage to crop yields and the global food supply.

### **Don 't look up**
Severe weather events are an indication of climate change, but are not themselves the underlying problem. Like the election of the president, they are severely problematic examples of dysfunction driven by systems besieged by long festering crises: corruption & money in politics helped enable the president, while a series of interrelated feedback loops have consistently accelerated climate change over the past generation.
Looking beyond the planetary symptoms to consider the underlying pathology leads to a further set of challenges that few in positions of institutional leadership have adequately considered.
Many stories, published by any number of news sources, have explored the unfolding El Nino in the South Pacific. Some have even considered its disturbing implications. Few, however, have placed it within the broader context of the climate crisis, considering it not only as a driver of predictable weather calamities, but as a reflection of shifting ocean currents that themselves hold massive implications for the longer term future.
Oscillations in the world's oceans are responsible for much of the movement that carries water and heat across them. Yet two of the most significant: the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) in the North Atlantic, and the Antarctica Circumpolar Current (ACC) near Antarctica, appear to be weakening due in large part to climate chaos.
As Dr. Morgan Sinclair recently [observed](https://substack.com/redirect/5f903c4e-390c-4f6a-8548-3e509f873bd1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) on this platform:
> Together these currents run a global "conveyor belt" of ocean water that both cools and warms the planet--releasing excess heat near the Arctic Circle while simultaneously warding off the next ice age by keeping the world warm enough that it doesn't freeze.
> Worldwide, north and south, the circulation of the seas is slowing down. That's trouble.
Dr. Sinclair goes on to explain in some detail how the AMOC and the ACC function, and why they matter so much.
Put simply, melting polar ice reduces the salinity of ocean water, which traditionally grew as water near the poles froze into ice. As the polar salinity pump diminishes, so does the force with which cold, salty water descends to the bottom of the ocean.
Scientists have long warned of the severe consequences of the ocean currents stalling. Hollywood directors have dramatized those consequences (for instance, in _The Day After Tomorrow_ , and _Waterworld_). Millions of young people around the world, driven by their awareness of preventable crisis, have taken to the streets to voice their demands for faster and more meaningful climate action.
Yet Washington stumbles in circles, while the AMOC and ACC continue to weaken, threatening crops & food supplies around the world.

### **Strap in**
Despite all the mounting attention to it, the El Niño brewing in the South Pacific will likely prove more destructive than anyone can possibly describe, only because its effects will cascade long beyond the season is over.
Mark Roberts recently [explained](https://open.substack.com/pub/markroberts995/p/scorched-harvest-the-strongest-el?r=97w99&utm_medium=ios) that:
> An El Niño is not a storm. It does not arrive with wind and fury and then recede. It is a reorganization of where rain falls on Earth, a slow, hemisphere-spanning transfer of moisture away from the croplands of Southeast Asia, southern Africa, Central America, and northeastern Brazil, and toward places that cannot use the rain to produce food such as the open Pacific, the deserts of coastal Peru, the flood plains of the Horn of Africa. _**The warm water is only the mechanism; the failed harvests are what people will actually live through.**_ Since the global food system runs on a handful of staple crops grown in a handful of climate-exposed regions, a sufficiently large _**El Ni ño is not a weather anomaly at all. It is going to be a global food shock on a twelve-month fuse.**_
This should be the lead story in every news publication on Earth. It should remain on the front page every day until elected leaders who have ignored this long-festering crisis are finally replaced.
To its credit, _the Guardian_ at least publishes opinion articles about the crisis. Today, Peter Gleich [wrote](https://substack.com/redirect/9dc5583e-d234-45f1-98fa-a071cbc23a71?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg):
> At any given moment, there are always places around the world suffering from droughts or floods or experiencing water scarcity - a normal consequence of the natural variability of our climate and weather.
> But what we're experiencing now is not normal; it is the direct consequence of accelerating human-caused climate changes, on top of decades of neglect and underinvestment in our water institutions and infrastructure.
> For years, climate scientists have warned that continued emissions of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels and other human activities would alter the planet's climate, raise temperatures, disrupt weather patterns and worsen extreme events, raise sea levels, and accelerate the spread of disease vectors. Those warnings were ignored, dismissed, downplayed. And now we are reaping what we've sown.
> Yet our politicians continue to prevaricate, refusing to take actions to protect water resources; or worse, rolling back earlier efforts.
Every day, journalists cover some aspect of the accelerating global climate catastrophe. Yet, even as eyes around the world turn towards some portion of the climate disaster forcing future generations into misery, the phenomenon as a whole--and its disturbing implications--seems to escape polite conversations, especially among policymakers.
Apologists for corporate rule within the Democratic party, for instance, [imagine](https://substack.com/redirect/b20a177a-5254-4787-a9dc-5a3a4a3ab168?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that climate is a divisive issue that is electorally inconvenient. But there is no more important issue to discuss.
The urgency of decisions that should have been made 20 years ago to protect the future grow increasingly insufficient as our leaders continue to bury their hands in the sand, and double down on a fossil fuel paradigm that threatens life on Earth.
> [| | | Shahid Buttar 1dHow are neither politicians, nor journalists, nor even voters, willing to consider the inescapable reality that should be driving their most urgent decisions?
> ---
> https://substack.com/@adammckay177538/note/c-311279990
> | 27| | 10|
> ---|---|---|---](https://substack.com/profile/15484941-shahid-buttar/note/c-312109637)
On the one hand, many institutions have grappled with the implications of climate chaos. The British insurance industry, for instance, conducted an analysis that predicted [4 billion deaths](https://open.substack.com/pub/rogerhallam/p/the-insurance-industry-predicts-mass?r=97w99&utm_medium=ios)--amounting to literally half of humanity--in the next century.
Meanwhile, major news outlets fawn over the president's [vanities](https://substack.com/@reedgalen/note/c-310251813?r=97w99&utm_medium=ios&utm_source=notes-share-action) rather than issues that will dramatically affect (or even end the lives of) billions of people.
### **Hands in the air**
I'll be honest: I have no idea how to overcome these patterns.
After dedicating years to direct action organizing, and more than half a decade to promoting better policies as a candidate for Congress, I learned the hard way that our system does not permit meaningful change. I've watched journalists and voters decide to preserve documented corruption at the cost of their own grandchildren's survival.
As far as I can tell, America's elected leaders, and the journalists who create cults of personality surrounding them, are oblivious. So, too, are voters who continue to send the same corporate shills back to Washington as if they hadn't engineered a preventable calamity that makes every other unfortunate event in human history look like a blessing by comparison.
As a writer and former candidate for public office, I've tried my best to [offer hope](https://substack.com/redirect/a9052d99-b998-4f53-8cfe-231087e87073?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to people concerned about the future. But [trying to conjure hope for young people](https://open.substack.com/pub/climatecasino/p/an-unexpected-message-from-the-edge?r=97w99&utm_medium=ios), in particular, has grown painfully futile. Many are more aware of the future crises that corrupt elected leaders have contrived than those leaders themselves.
I've been relatively publicly silent lately. But that's not because I can't find issues to write about.
Sadly, every day offers new horrors that have led me to start dozens of half-drafted articles. The problem constraining me is that, as a writer, I have always offered my ideas with an eye towards a broader process. My aims have included informing people, inspiring them, and building grassroots social movements to force our shared concerns into political institutions.
But America's corruption makes that process appear like a cruel joke. I wish I could offer you hope. But I have a hard time lying.
That said, I can at least share a little information, and a few ideas that could still make a difference.
### **None of this is rocket science**
Faced with catastrophic risks to life on Earth, a sane civilization might consider alternatives that would lead to greater sustainability.
Capitalism, however, is not sane. Capital is rapacious, even to the point of destroying the people who wield it.
Given the relationship between the Pentagon and climate chaos, the very first thing we might do to address the climate catastrophe would be to stop investing in its expansion. Reducing the military budget is a long overdue no-brainer.
Shifting some of those resources recovered from the military budget to climate resilience would make even more sense. Among the many possibilities that come to mind--such as organizing [controlled burns](https://substack.com/redirect/312620f8-f72f-49e2-8842-c1c4026ab8a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) during the winter season to reduce the propensity of severe fires in the summer and fall, municipal [composting systems](https://substack.com/redirect/abbf271c-cf4e-4533-a182-7e328c311fb7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to reduce waste and reuse bio-resources, and a youth jobs corp dedicated to cultivating local permaculture & sustainability projects--few seem as pressing as simply paying firefighters what they're worth.
Across the country, firefighters are currently confronting the leading edge of the climate crisis. Like military servicemembers, they spend weeks or months on the road, facing severe risks to their life and health while away from their families.
Many work without adequate support from local, state, or federal governments. Some are forced to [buy their own equipment](https://substack.com/redirect/0a83d4a2-57aa-408a-b638-c0e8c181da92?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
On the one hand, federal firefighters received [a long overdue raise](https://substack.com/redirect/aeded907-d24c-4f9a-821d-0c3d567d1f69?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) last year. On the other hand, a [recruiting crisis](https://substack.com/redirect/2af2ffa3-383e-4d65-8cb8-9d20dc7e0350?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) continues across the country, suggesting that resources currently funding weapons, or military recruitment--or local policing, for that matter--could find better uses.
Finally, nationalizing the fossil fuel industry is a crucial step in removing the powerful incentive of corporate profit from the scale. I've argued before that allowing the extraction of non-renewable resources for profit forces the future to subsidize the present. It is a recipe for civilizational self-destruction.
Nationalizing the sector--by allowing extraction only by public agencies that do not pursue profit--should have happened decades ago. Of course, any other country that has attempted to pursue that path has faced a [CIA coup in retaliation](https://substack.com/redirect/e48823c1-9aa5-4c73-bbab-09b7a1e829e7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), so I have little hope that Washington will permit that policy to see the light of day in the U.S.
But the future of life on Earth increasingly depends on it. As long as capital is allowed to profit from fossil fuel extraction, human beings will all remain reduced to its fodder.

China has evacuated over a million people fleeing floods inundating major cities including Shanghai, while wildfires burning near Madrid and Paris have prompted alarm and anxiety across Europe. The juxtaposition, however, suggests a whole far worse than the sum of its parts. International agencies and non-profit organizations have spared no alarm. The United Nations Environment Programme, for instance, has noted that "The world may soon cross some potentially disastrous tipping points," and powerfully depicted the scale of climate chaos through . Yet, while these globally interlinked unfolding disasters have attracted worldwide attention and concern, the pattern that connects them continues to be effectively ignored by elected leaders and journalists across the United States. | | ---|---|--- Cartoon by A war making everything worse The war in Iran is offensive for many reasons. The that enabled it will be remembered by whatever vestiges of human civilization survive the next generation. Its damage to the global economy continues to mount by the day. But the relationship between war and the acceleration of climate chaos is, in fact, the dumbest thing about the whole sordid endeavor. Ultimately, the Pentagon is the Earth's fossil fuels, while its actions--particularly in the Middle East over the past six months--have made fossil fuels more scarce, and less secure to extract or ship. Beyond this long applicable global analysis of the Pentagon's carbon footprint, Trump's war on Iran has also sparked an acute over the past six months, which has already done incalculable damage to crop yields and the global food supply. To support my work, please consider becoming a paid subscriber. Don 't look up Severe weather events are an indication of climate change, but are not themselves the underlying problem. Like the election of the president, they are severely problematic examples of dysfunction driven by systems besieged by long festering crises: corruption & money in politics helped enable the president, while a series of interrelated feedback loops have consistently accelerated climate change over the past generation. Looking beyond the planetary symptoms to consider the underlying pathology leads to a further set of challenges that few in positions of institutional leadership have adequately considered. Many stories, published by any number of news sources, have explored the unfolding El Nino in the South Pacific. Some have even considered its disturbing implications. Few, however, have placed it within the broader context of the climate crisis, considering it not only as a driver of predictable weather calamities, but as a reflection of shifting ocean currents that themselves hold massive implications for the longer term future. Oscillations in the world's oceans are responsible for much of the movement that carries water and heat across them. Yet two of the most significant: the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) in the North Atlantic, and the Antarctica Circumpolar Current (ACC) near Antarctica, appear to be weakening due in large part to climate chaos. As Dr. Morgan Sinclair recently on this platform: Together these currents run a global "conveyor belt" of ocean water that both cools and warms the planet--releasing excess heat near the Arctic Circle while simultaneously warding off the next ice age by keeping the world warm enough that it doesn't freeze. Worldwide, north and south, the circulation of the seas is slowing down. That's trouble. Dr. Sinclair goes on to explain in some detail how the AMOC and the ACC function, and why they matter so much. Put simply, melting polar ice reduces the salinity of ocean water, which traditionally grew as water near the poles froze into ice. As the polar salinity pump diminishes, so does the force with which cold, salty water descends to the bottom of the ocean. Scientists have long warned of the severe consequences of the ocean currents stalling. Hollywood directors have dramatized those consequences (for instance, in The Day After Tomorrow , and Waterworld). Millions of young people around the world, driven by their awareness of preventable crisis, have taken to the streets to voice their demands for faster and more meaningful climate action. Yet Washington stumbles in circles, while the AMOC and ACC continue to weaken, threatening crops & food supplies around the world. Strap in Despite all the mounting attention to it, the El Niño brewing in the South Pacific will likely prove more destructive than anyone can possibly describe, only because its effects will cascade long beyond the season is over. Mark Roberts recently that: An El Niño is not a storm. It does not arrive with wind and fury and then recede. It is a reorganization of where rain falls on Earth, a slow, hemisphere-spanning transfer of moisture away from the croplands of Southeast Asia, southern Africa, Central America, and northeastern Brazil, and toward places that cannot use the rain to produce food such as the open Pacific, the deserts of coastal Peru, the flood plains of the Horn of Africa. The warm water is only the mechanism; the failed harvests are what people will actually live through. Since the global food system runs on a handful of staple crops grown in a handful of climate-exposed regions, a sufficiently large El Ni ño is not a weather anomaly at all. It is going to be a global food shock on a twelve-month fuse. This should be the lead story in every news publication on Earth. It should remain on the front page every day until elected leaders who have ignored this long-festering crisis are finally replaced. To its credit, the Guardian at least publishes opinion articles about the crisis. Today, Peter Gleich : At any given moment, there are always places around the world suffering from droughts or floods or experiencing water scarcity - a normal consequence of the natural variability of our climate and weather. But what we're experiencing now is not normal; it is the direct consequence of accelerating human-caused climate changes, on top of decades of neglect and underinvestment in our water institutions and infrastructure. For years, climate scientists have warned that continued emissions of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels and other human activities would alter the planet's climate, raise temperatures, disrupt weather patterns and worsen extreme events, raise sea levels, and accelerate the spread of disease vectors. Those warnings were ignored, dismissed, downplayed. And now we are reaping what we've sown. Yet our politicians continue to prevaricate, refusing to take actions to protect water resources; or worse, rolling back earlier efforts. Every day, journalists cover some aspect of the accelerating global climate catastrophe. Yet, even as eyes around the world turn towards some portion of the climate disaster forcing future generations into misery, the phenomenon as a whole--and its disturbing implications--seems to escape polite conversations, especially among policymakers. Apologists for corporate rule within the Democratic party, for instance, that climate is a divisive issue that is electorally inconvenient. But there is no more important issue to discuss. The urgency of decisions that should have been made 20 years ago to protect the future grow increasingly insufficient as our leaders continue to bury their hands in the sand, and double down on a fossil fuel paradigm that threatens life on Earth. On the one hand, many institutions have grappled with the implications of climate chaos. The British insurance industry, for instance, conducted an analysis that predicted to literally half of humanity--in the next century. Meanwhile, major news outlets fawn over the president's rather than issues that will dramatically affect (or even end the lives of) billions of people. Hands in the air I'll be honest: I have no idea how to overcome these patterns. After dedicating years to direct action organizing, and more than half a decade to promoting better policies as a candidate for Congress, I learned the hard way that our system does not permit meaningful change. I've watched journalists and voters decide to preserve documented corruption at the cost of their own grandchildren's survival. As far as I can tell, America's elected leaders, and the journalists who create cults of personality surrounding them, are oblivious. So, too, are voters who continue to send the same corporate shills back to Washington as if they hadn't engineered a preventable calamity that makes every other unfortunate event in human history look like a blessing by comparison. As a writer and former candidate for public office, I've tried my best to to people concerned about the future. But , in particular, has grown painfully futile. Many are more aware of the future crises that corrupt elected leaders have contrived than those leaders themselves. I've been relatively publicly silent lately. But that's not because I can't find issues to write about. Sadly, every day offers new horrors that have led me to start dozens of half-drafted articles. The problem constraining me is that, as a writer, I have always offered my ideas with an eye towards a broader process. My aims have included informing people, inspiring them, and building grassroots social movements to force our shared concerns into political institutions. But America's corruption makes that process appear like a cruel joke. I wish I could offer you hope. But I have a hard time lying. That said, I can at least share a little information, and a few ideas that could still make a difference. None of this is rocket science Faced with catastrophic risks to life on Earth, a sane civilization might consider alternatives that would lead to greater sustainability. Capitalism, however, is not sane. Capital is rapacious, even to the point of destroying the people who wield it. Given the relationship between the Pentagon and climate chaos, the very first thing we might do to address the climate catastrophe would be to stop investing in its expansion. Reducing the military budget is a long overdue no-brainer. Shifting some of those resources recovered from the military budget to climate resilience would make even more sense. Among the many possibilities that come to mind--such as organizing during the winter season to reduce the propensity of severe fires in the summer and fall, municipal to reduce waste and reuse bio-resources, and a youth jobs corp dedicated to cultivating local permaculture & sustainability projects--few seem as pressing as simply paying firefighters what they're worth. Across the country, firefighters are currently confronting the leading edge of the climate crisis. Like military servicemembers, they spend weeks or months on the road, facing severe risks to their life and health while away from their families. Many work without adequate support from local, state, or federal governments. Some are forced to . On the one hand, federal firefighters received last year. On the other hand, a continues across the country, suggesting that resources currently funding weapons, or military recruitment--or local policing, for that matter--could find better uses. Finally, nationalizing the fossil fuel industry is a crucial step in removing the powerful incentive of corporate profit from the scale. I've argued before that allowing the extraction of non-renewable resources for profit forces the future to subsidize the present. It is a recipe for civilizational self-destruction. Nationalizing the sector--by allowing extraction only by public agencies that do not pursue profit--should have happened decades ago. Of course, any other country that has attempted to pursue that path has faced a , so I have little hope that Washington will permit that policy to see the light of day in the U.S. But the future of life on Earth increasingly depends on it. As long as capital is allowed to profit from fossil fuel extraction, human beings will all remain reduced to its fodder. ## Robocalls Reach Highest Level in a Year
Robocalls are [spiking nationwide](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLHO3CAQhJ_G7jgtGBv_BUUad3_alBYHa7PJ2iDg7uS3j5xXSDkzmtHo-_W9fjtiOvef7kDbtrSe-KmMrWFZW3kduaJ_FWpX5nTVxK6g51WBmgTMQqrV-UZvXLXrg90QFQ49WmnmaVRfyox9tPPwFQLAc5u1ktoZM5gA4-gGqZ0GJ3uy9x7MUkkAM-pHGGcA8GbyPqAH2WnAQC2Vx-9EZ4u48ZXeWB4-HT3b2Fqu3fCjU0unlhYxEvOddWrJiclft40-nonTfosJFJhZipKeyTvmKlxBUTP9oXMXWDN6csyX2FIROaYTxfk6nliq-FCLokWseHec8Clg7dTSFxvyh5ipTqbTsB-O_p3o239yfVv1NwAA__--uY-l), with Americans fielding more spam calls in July than in any month in the past year, according to call-screening service YouMail. The tally topped [4.3 billion calls](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkb2upDAMhZ8GOqMQws8UFNtMd7fdEmUcz5CrkCDHGZa3XzHFvsAtLft81qfz52v5sj74-PptN5rlmZZIRw4kQrwIl23PhIW9nHtIZ07BMmFYtNIDqAlavVgU_6bF2NrNTyJNXU1zO05Dr2967Ot1to8OO31rezWNQ-uG3uBDmf52I3wiDar288VTU6tbpcbeNK6flFI4DoiOULWVUeS8JG6-k4-y0jOc6U3cYNrqMK8ie666X5W-V_p-HEez86VxeKbrpNL3awSmQDZTrvS9ZOD0SGhDyIApio-FoOyHZQfCFB3YzyKXjfiKIvk3OdgSE8hqIxjo4OFD8CmCj_BdwgkWMbHz8QWS4Exlsz78fwQ-OvoLndKTMeNkmlW2UPPs9uPC5GGsjHpdkY-X_LCO96z_BQAA___tSqU6) in a single month, and the most common was a fake "pre-approved" loan offer promising big money at low payments. YouMail calls it illegal telemarketing at scale and likely a scam. Numbers with Houston's 346 area code saw the sharpest jump, up 19% in one month, followed by codes covering Atlanta and Albany in Georgia, and much of Indiana and Tennessee. But no region was spared. A bill cracking down on overseas robocalls recently passed the Senate. Until then, experts say: Don't pick up. Let unknown numbers go to voicemail, and always call your bank back on the number printed on your card, not the one that called you.
